summary: Updates RFC 6775, 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery, to clarify its role as a registration technique and simplify registration in 6LoWPAN routers. It also adds registration capabilities and mobility enhancements.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8505 updates address registration for IPv6 over low-power wireless networks. Routers can compare registration updates, support a node that moves, and let a proxy register an address for another node.

subtitle: Address registration for low-power IPv6 networks, with support for movement, proxies and ownership checks.

tldr.problem: RFC 6775 provides address registration for 6LoWPAN networks, but does not identify the newest registration when a node moves and ties its ownership field to an EUI-64 value.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8505 extends the registration option with a Transaction ID, a Registration Ownership Verifier, reachability signaling, new status values, and registration of a target address by a node or proxy.
tldr.outcome: The update supports movement, proxy registration, and privacy addresses while retaining compatibility with RFC 6775-only nodes under specified conditions. RFC 8505 updates RFC 6775 and has itself been updated by RFC 8928, RFC 8929, RFC 9010, RFC 9685 and RFC 9926.

today: RFC 8505 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6775. It has been updated by RFC 8928, RFC 8929, RFC 9010, RFC 9685 and RFC 9926, and the metadata does not list a document that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why 6LoWPAN Registration Is Extended
sections.content:
IPv6 Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) can use star or mesh topologies. RFC 6775 defines a registration mechanism and an IPv6 Neighbor Discovery registrar to help keep addresses unique while reducing reliance on multicast and broadcast.

RFC 8505 updates that mechanism. It adds support for detecting a node's most recent location, registering through a proxy, and handling privacy and temporary addresses. A router that accepts registrations needs storage for every address that may be registered, including addresses not currently sending traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Low-power IPv6 devices register their addresses with nearby routers. This update helps the network track moves and lets one node register an address for another.

sections.title: Nodes That Register and Keep State
sections.content:
A 6LoWPAN Node (6LN) registers an address with a 6LoWPAN Router (6LR). A 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR) keeps registration information for the domain. The node that owns the address is the Registered Node; the Registering Node sends the registration and may be a proxy.

An IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Registrar processes the registration and returns its status. A Routing Registrar also provides reachability for the registered address, for example through routing or proxy Neighbor Discovery. A Backbone Router is a Routing Registrar that connects multiple LLNs over a backbone link.
sections.plainLanguage: A node asks a router to register its address. A border router keeps domain-wide information, and a proxy can send a registration for another node.

sections.title: The Extended Address Registration Option
sections.content:
The Extended Address Registration Option (EARO) updates the Address Registration Option used in Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages. It carries a Registration Lifetime, a Transaction ID (TID), a Registration Ownership Verifier (ROVR), and flags. The R flag requests that a Routing Registrar provide reachability for the address; the T flag indicates that the TID is present.

The ROVR replaces the earlier EUI-64 field and can carry different kinds of identifiers. It is 64 bits when backward compatibility is needed; otherwise, it may be 128, 192, or 256 bits. The RFC also extends duplicate-address messages to carry the TID and ROVR and adds capability bits to the 6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option.
sections.plainLanguage: The EARO carries the address registration, a counter for comparing updates, and a value used to match ownership. Its flags can request reachability services.

sections.title: Comparing Updates and Matching Ownership
sections.content:
The node increments the TID when it re-registers. Routers compare TIDs to decide which registration is more recent and where a moving node is currently reachable. When a node registers with multiple routers in parallel, it uses the same TID for those registrations.

The TID uses a one-byte lollipop counter with a comparison window of 16. The ROVR lets routers match attempts to register the same IPv6 address. It must not be used to link registrations for different addresses, and a node should keep it in persistent memory so it can re-register after a reboot.
sections.plainLanguage: A newer TID helps routers identify a node's latest registration after movement. The ROVR helps match updates for one address to its original registration.

sections.title: Registering, Moving and Removing Addresses
sections.content:
The address being registered appears in the Target Address field of the Neighbor Solicitation. A registration also includes a Source Link-Layer Address option. A proxy can use this mechanism to register a target address on another node's behalf.

A link-local address needs to be unique only between the two nodes using it, so its registration does not require the duplicate-address exchange between a 6LR and 6LBR. A node registers a link-local address first if it has no registered address. It renews registrations with a new solicitation and can end one by sending a lifetime of 0. When moving, it should register with a new 6LR using an incremented TID; a Moved status can trigger cleanup at the old location.
sections.plainLanguage: A registration names its target address, whether the node sends it or a proxy does. When a node moves, the new registration carries a newer counter so routers can update the old location.

sections.title: Working with RFC 6775-Only Devices
sections.content:
An updated node must use an EARO, but it behaves in a backward-compatible way when it does not know that a router supports RFC 8505. The updated node learns support from the 6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option in Router Advertisements. Without that indication, it treats the router as RFC 6775-only.

When communicating with an RFC 6775-only router, the updated node uses a 64-bit ROVR. An updated router must accept a valid RFC 6775-style registration. An older border router can process the extended duplicate-address message when the ROVR is 64 bits; the updated router uses the leftmost 64 bits in that message.
sections.plainLanguage: Updated nodes and routers can work with RFC 6775-only devices if they use the compatible registration form. Capability information tells a node when to use the newer behavior.

sections.title: Security, Resource Limits and Address Privacy
sections.content:
The LLN MAC layer must provide secure unicast to and from a Routing Registrar, and secure broadcast or multicast from it, to prevent tampering with or replaying Neighbor Discovery messages. The network must ensure that only authorized devices act as border routers or Routing Registrars. TIDs and de-registration help detect stale state, but the RFC leaves address-ownership protection methods outside its scope.

Routers should limit registrations as a protective measure while retaining capacity for multiple addresses per node. The required minimum capacity ranges from 3 addresses for a very constrained LLN to 10 for a larger device. The RFC does not limit how many addresses a device may form and discourages deriving a link-local interface identifier from EUI-64 because that prevents some privacy techniques.
sections.plainLanguage: The link layer must protect registration messages from changes and replay. Only authorized routers should hold registration state, and resource limits must still allow several addresses per node.
